strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and timely gap: horizon-aware (deadline-constrained) anytime-valid tests and confidence sequences, building on the betting/e-process framework. The formulation of horizon-aware betting as a finite-horizon optimal control problem over the state space (t, log W_t) is clean and clarifying.

The theoretical contributions (Theorem 3.1, Propositions 3.4 and 3.6) provide genuine insight: a 'tubular interior' result showing near-optimal policies must stay close to Kelly when on schedule, and type-based large-deviation sufficient conditions for when aggressive (behind schedule) or defensive (ahead of schedule) betting beats Kelly. Proofs are included in the appendix and appear correct, using appropriate tools (Hoeffding's lemma, Ville's inequality, Sanov's theorem).

The empirical Kelly estimate, hedging over epsilon-schedules, and the DQN policy all preserve anytime-validity by construction (predictability + Ville's inequality), so the learning component cannot break the statistical guarantees — an important and correctly handled design point.

The paper is well organized and honest about limitations: it clearly states that the theory gives only partial characterization, that experiments focus on Beta/Beta-mixture families, and that extension to other distributions is future work. Reproducibility is strong: full DQN hyperparameters, feature design, training distribution, and implementation details (including two-sided adaptation of the STaR baseline) are provided.

The phase diagram (Figure 2) computed via exact oracle DP, and its qualitative recovery by the learned DQN policy (Figure 3), is a convincing and interpretable validation of the theory-to-practice pipeline.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are partial and somewhat restricted: Theorem 3.1's second part only constrains policies that deviate from Kelly for a fixed fraction of steps, and Propositions 3.4/3.6 compare only constant-betting strategies under finite-support assumptions. Thus the headline qualitative claims (aggressive better when behind, defensive better when ahead) are supported only under these restricted conditions, and the connection to the adaptive policies actually deployed is informal.

The gap between theory and the proposed method is significant: the sufficient conditions involve rate functions (I+, I-) that depend on the unknown PX, and the DQN operates on heuristic features with no performance guarantee. The DQN's advantage over the simple hedged epsilon-schedule baseline appears empirically modest in several settings (e.g., Figure 3), so the added complexity of deep RL is not always clearly justified.

Empirical evaluation is narrow: all experiments use Beta or Beta-mixture distributions with N in [100, 350] and 5000 repetitions. No results on real data, non-Beta distributions, discrete/Bernoulli data (which the theory heavily leans on), or larger horizons. Generalization of the universal DQN beyond its training distribution family is untested.

The comparison against Voracek & Orabona (2025) requires a nontrivial adaptation of their one-sided STaR method to the two-sided setting; the fairness of this adapted baseline is uncertain, and no sensitivity analysis of this choice is provided.

Some illustrative examples use unrealistic scales (e.g., Example 3.3 with T = 50000 and log-wealth gap of 1475), which weakens the practical relevance of the theorem's conditions; the regime in which the theory's quantitative constants are meaningful appears far from the experimental settings (N = 100).

strengths: The problem is well motivated and the framing of horizon-aware betting as a finite-horizon optimal control problem over the (t, log Wt) plane is natural and clear; the resulting three-regime 'phase diagram' intuition (Kelly / fractional-Kelly / aggressive) is interpretable and pedagogically useful.

Validity is preserved by construction: all proposed procedures are predictable bets in Λm, so the level-α guarantee follows from Ville's inequality regardless of how the policy is learned. This is a genuine methodological advantage over many learned-procedure pipelines.

The paper is honest about the partial nature of its theory: Theorem 3.1 and Propositions 3.4/3.6 are explicitly presented as sufficient conditions / partial characterizations rather than a full solution of the Bellman recursion.

Reproducibility is treated reasonably well: hyperparameters, network architecture, training distribution, exploration schedule, and implementation details (including the two-sided adaptation of STaR baselines) are documented in Appendices C–E, and training cost is disclosed.
weaknesses: There is a substantial gap between the theory and the regime in which the experiments are run. The quantitative conditions of Theorem 3.1 only become informative for very large T (Example 3.3 uses T = 50,000 to get a nontrivial bound), while all headline experiments use N = 100–350. Similarly, Propositions 3.4/3.6 require finite alphabets and knowledge of PX-dependent KL rate functions I±(λ, r) that are unobservable in practice. As a result, the theoretical results provide qualitative intuition only, and never actually certify or explain behavior in the experimental setting.

The empirical evaluation is too narrow to support the 'state-of-the-art' claim. All experiments use Beta or Beta-mixture distributions — the same family the DQN is trained on — so the evaluation is essentially in-distribution, which materially weakens any generalization claim. The conclusion itself concedes that experiments 'have focused on the Beta family,' but no out-of-family results (e.g., Bernoulli, discrete, heavy-tailed bounded variables, real data) are provided.

The main comparison baseline (STaR-Bets / STaR-Hoeffding of Voráček & Orabona, 2025) is designed for one-sided tests and is adapted by the authors to the two-sided case. This adaptation's quality is not validated, so the reported gains over the closest prior work could reflect a suboptimal baseline rather than a genuine advantage of the proposed method.

The reported performance improvements are modest in absolute terms (e.g., confidence widths of 0.066 vs 0.079 vs 0.141 at N = 100 in Figure 4) and are shown without uncertainty quantification in the power plots (Figure 3), making it hard to judge whether the differences are statistically meaningful at 5,000 repetitions.

The DQN component is not connected to the theory in any rigorous way: the policy is justified only by the informal phase diagram and qualitative agreement of modal-action maps. Given the three-action set {λ̂/2, λ̂, λend} and 22 hand-crafted features, it remains unclear whether the learned policy is meaningfully better than simpler schedule-aware heuristics across a broader benchmark, and no ablation over feature groups or action sets is provided.

The paper claims the learned phase diagram is 'state-dependent and distribution-sensitive,' but the evidence is pathwise visualizations and modal-action maps on selected configurations; no quantitative measure of policy adaptivity or comparison against a fixed-schedule policy across a systematic grid of difficulties is given.

Presentation issues: several typos and formatting errors (e.g., '1 − 2 × 10^{-t}' in Example 3.3, 'a the fully time-uniform procedures', mangled author names 'Vora´cek'), and the 'phase diagram' of Figure 1 is admittedly informal, which risks overstating the definitiveness of the theoretical contribution.

strengths: The core idea—casting horizon-aware betting as a finite-horizon optimal control problem over the (t, log W_t) plane—is natural, novel relative to the prior STaR work of Voraček & Orabona (2025), and yields an interpretable three-regime phase diagram.

The theoretical results are honestly scoped and the proofs (Hoeffding/Ville for Theorem 3.1, Sanov/type-based arguments for Propositions 3.4 and 3.6 in Appendices B.2–B.3) appear correct; Lemma A.3 is a clean technical contribution connecting infinite-alphabet rate functions to type-based ones.

Validity is preserved by construction: bets are predictable and clipped to Λ_m, so the learned policy cannot compromise anytime-valid guarantees—this is a genuinely sound design choice for combining RL with safe inference, and the paper argues it clearly.

The universal DQN, trained once on synthetic episodes over randomized (N, m, µ), is an interesting and practical design; the modal-action maps qualitatively recover the oracle phase diagrams (Figure 3 vs Figure 2), supporting the claim of state-dependent, distribution-sensitive adaptation rather than a fixed schedule.
The hedging-over-ε-schedules baseline (Appendix C) is a simple, valid, and useful contribution in its own right, with a small log K cost.

The limitations discussion is honest (e.g., experiments restricted to the Beta family), and reproducibility details (features, hyperparameters, training procedure in Appendices D–E) are unusually thorough.
weaknesses: There is a substantial gap between the theory and the experimental regime. Theorem 3.1's interior-region guarantees require very large horizons (Example 3.3 uses T = 50,000), while all experiments use N ≤ 350; conditions (3) and (5) in Propositions 3.4/3.6 are also not verified to hold in the tested settings. The phase-diagram narrative is thus supported qualitatively (via oracle DP and DQN action maps), not by the formal results at practical horizons.

The theoretical results only cover constant-bet policies and finite-support distributions; they provide no approximation or performance guarantee for the learned DQN policy, whose superiority remains purely empirical.

The evaluation scope is narrow: all data-generating distributions are Beta or Beta-mixtures, which coincide with the DQN's training family. Generalization to other distributions, heavier tails, or real A/B-test data is untested and left to future work, weakening the claimed state-of-the-art status.

Improvement margins over baselines are sometimes small and not accompanied by significance analysis (e.g., Figure 4b: DQN width 0.134 vs STaR-Bets 0.141), and the STaR baselines require the authors' own two-sided adaptation, which may disadvantage them.

The DQN's gains over the much simpler hedged ε-schedule heuristic are modest in several settings, raising the question of how much of the benefit comes from RL versus simple schedule-awareness plus hedging; an ablation isolating this (e.g., hedged schedules over a richer schedule class) is not provided.
Only three discrete actions are considered ({λ̂/2, λ̂, λ_end}); the restriction is justified by interpretability, but the paper does not examine sensitivity to this action set.

No code release is mentioned despite the heavy empirical component, and the paper lacks discussion of the computational cost of running the DQN per test relative to simple closed-form betting strategies.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framing: horizon-aware (deadline-constrained) anytime-valid testing is cast as a finite-horizon optimal control problem over the (t, log W_t) state space, a perspective distinct from prior work such as Voráček & Orabona (2025) and Koning & Van Meer (2026), and clearly positioned relative to both.

Validity is preserved by construction: all proposed policies (hedged ε-greedy schedules, DQN) use predictable bets in Λ_m, so anytime-validity follows from Ville's inequality regardless of how the policy is learned. The hedging-over-schedules construction (Appendix C) is simple, correct, and costs only an additive log K in log-wealth.

Useful partial theoretical characterization: Theorem 3.1 formalizes a 'tubular' near-schedule region where deviations from Kelly are provably suboptimal (via Hoeffding and Ville-type arguments), and Propositions 3.4/3.6 give sufficient Sanov-based conditions for aggressive/defensive bets to outperform Kelly. The examples (3.3, 3.5, 3.7) concretely illustrate when the theory applies.

Unusual breadth of evaluation: oracle phase diagrams, rejection-probability curves, confidence sequence widths, OOD transfer (logit-normal), a separate Bernoulli control/RL experiment, longer deadlines, alternative significance levels, and six real datasets (DNA methylation, humidity) with explicit Type-I error calibration checks. Type-I error stays below α throughout, as guaranteed.

Reproducibility of the method is well supported: full DQN architecture, state features, training distribution, and hyperparameters are documented (Table 1), including honest negative results (9-action ablation gives no overall improvement). Limitations, including interpretability and the continuous-distribution focus, are acknowledged candidly.
weaknesses: Theory–practice gap: the main sufficient-condition results (Propositions 3.4, 3.6) and Lemma A.3 require a finite alphabet X, yet the flagship experiments use continuous distributions (Beta, Beta-mixtures, real data). The paper does not explain how the finite-alphabet theory transfers to this setting, so the headline 'phase diagram' insights are only informally connected to the experiments.

The central claims about the learned policy are empirical only. There is no guarantee (even a regret-style bound) that the DQN policy is near-optimal for the stated objective (1); 'state-of-the-art results' rests entirely on simulations. Moreover, the oracle DP and phase diagrams require knowledge of the true P_X (population Kelly bet), which is unavailable in practice, so the diagnostic structure the DQN is claimed to 'recover' is oracle-level.

Gains over baselines are modest and not uniform. In several real-data panels (e.g., Figures 9–14), STaR-Hoeffding or the hedged ε-schedule match or beat DQN, and DQN is best in 5/6 rather than all cases. Power differences in Figures 3–7 are visible but sometimes small relative to the added complexity and loss of interpretability.

The DQN policy is evaluated on a very small action set {λ̂/2, λ̂, λ_end} chosen to match the three-regime intuition; this partially bakes in the paper's own qualitative theory, weakening the claim that the RL agent 'learns' the phase structure rather than inheriting it from the action design and feature engineering (22 hand-crafted predictable features).

The comparison to STaR-Bets requires a nontrivial adaptation of a one-sided method to the two-sided setting (sign-switching rule in Appendix D); the fairness and optimality of this adaptation for the baseline is not analyzed.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the 'Code:' field on page 1 appears empty, and no code or artifact link is provided, despite the heavy RL component whose outcome depends on seeds, checkpointing, and training dynamics.

The Bellman recursion and stopping-time formulation assume a known null m with the test repeated for all m; the paper does not discuss the multiplicity/coverage subtleties of intersecting infinitely many such tests beyond citing the standard duality, and computational cost of the continuum of hypothesis tests is not addressed.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically relevant gap in the anytime-valid inference literature: existing betting-based tests and confidence sequences (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas 2024, Orabona & Jun 2024, etc.) assume an infinite stream, while many applications have a hard sample-size deadline. The framing of horizon-aware betting as a finite-horizon optimal control problem over (t, log Wt) is clean and natural.

The theoretical contributions are honestly scoped and rigorous. Theorem 3.1 gives an interpretable 'on-schedule' characterization (Kelly bets are near-optimal; significant deviations suffer a provable drift deficit) with a complete proof via Hoeffding/Ville arguments, and Propositions 3.4 and 3.6 give sufficient conditions for aggressive/defensive bets to outperform Kelly, with careful finite-T correction terms derived via type-based Sanov arguments (Lemma A.3). The worked examples (3.3, 3.5, 3.7) concretely verify the conditions.

Validity is preserved by construction: all proposed policies (hedged epsilon-schedules, DQN) use predictable bets clipped to Λm, so anytime-validity holds regardless of how the policy is learned. The hedging-over-schedules section correctly uses convex mixtures of test martingales, and the log-K price of hedging is explicitly quantified.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough: oracle DP phase diagrams validating the theory, deadline-limited power curves, confidence sequence widths, alternative reward shaping (DQN-EB/DQN-U), out-of-distribution transfer (logit-normal), a separate Bernoulli-family training run, extended horizons (N up to 350), different α, action-space ablation, explicit Type-I error calibration checks, and real-data experiments on two distinct domains (DNA methylation, relative humidity) with 5/6 wins without fine-tuning.

Reproducibility is well supported: full DQN architecture, feature description (22 predictable features), complete hyperparameter table, training protocol, and details for adapting STaR baselines to the two-sided setting.
The paper discusses limitations candidly (interpretability of learned policies, focus on continuous distributions, gap between oracle DP and practical state features) without overselling.
weaknesses: There is a substantial gap between the theory and the method. The phase diagram results are proven under restrictive assumptions (finite support with |X| = k for Propositions 3.4/3.6; the striking Example 3.3 uses T = 50000, far beyond the N = 100 regimes actually evaluated), while the deployed DQN uses only a 3-action set {λbt/2, λbt, λmax} with hand-engineered features. The theory motivates but does not formally justify the learned policy, and no regret or optimality guarantee is given for it. The central 'SOTA' claim rests on empirics rather than on the theory.

The sufficient conditions in Propositions 3.4 and 3.6 are admittedly conservative (constant-bet policies, finite-T corrections, finite alphabets), so the 'phase diagram' in Figure 1 is qualitative rather than a precise characterization of the optimal policy; the paper acknowledges the DP is intractable in general, but the resulting theory is a collection of partial results rather than a sharp understanding of the finite-horizon betting problem.

The comparison against the only prior horizon-aware baseline (STaR-Bets/STaR-Hoeffding, Voráček & Orabona 2025) involves the authors' own two-sided adaptation using the sign of the current mean estimate (Appendix D). This adaptation is plausible but heuristic, and since STaR was designed for one-sided tests, the reported gaps over STaR could partly reflect the adaptation rather than a fundamental advantage; a sensitivity analysis of this choice is not provided.

The practical gains, while consistent, are modest in several regimes (e.g., Figure 3b where all methods are near 0.15–0.25 rejection probability; Figure 15 shows a 9-action space gives no overall improvement), suggesting the learned-policy machinery may be near a plateau given the action discretization and feature set; the paper's explanation for the 9-action result is speculative.
The 'Code:' placeholder on page 1 is empty, so no code/artifact link is actually provided in the manuscript, which weakens reproducibility claims despite the detailed experimental descriptions.

Some presentation issues: the main-text flow jumps between oracle DP analysis (which requires knowing PX), hedging heuristics, and DQN, making the logical dependency of the final method on the theory somewhat loose; several key claims (e.g., 'yields state-of-the-art results' in the abstract) are stronger than what limited baselines on Beta-family and resampled real data can firmly establish, particularly given the i.i.d. assumption excludes the temporal dependence present in the motivating humidity data.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically relevant gap: standard anytime-valid procedures are time-uniform over an indefinite horizon, whereas many applications have a hard deadline N. Formalizing horizon-aware betting as a finite-horizon optimal control problem over the state space (t, log Wt) is a natural and novel framing relative to prior work (Waudby-Smith & Ramdas 2024; Voracek & Orabona 2025; Koning & Van Meer 2026).

The theoretical results, while partial, are meaningful: Theorem 3.1 proves that in a 'tubular' interior region near-schedule policies deviating from Kelly are provably suboptimal (Hoeffding/Ville-based arguments), and Propositions 3.4 and 3.6 give sufficient conditions (via type-based/Sanov large-deviation analysis) under which aggressive betting when behind schedule and defensive betting when ahead of schedule beat Kelly. The proofs in Appendices B.1-B.3 and Lemma A.3 appear correct and self-contained, and the worked examples (3.3, 3.5, 3.7) help verify the conditions are non-vacuous.

Anytime-validity is preserved by construction throughout: all learned policies map to predictable bets in the constrained set Lambda_m, and hedging over epsilon-schedules is a convex mixture of test martingales, so Ville's inequality applies regardless of how the policy was chosen. This is a clean separation between learning and validity.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough: oracle DP phase diagrams that visually validate the theory, rejection-probability comparisons against STaR-Bets/STaR-Hoeffding and horizon-agnostic baselines, confidence sequence widths, reward-shaping ablations (DQN-EB, DQN-U), action-space ablation, extended horizons (N up to 350), alpha = 0.01, out-of-distribution evaluation on logit-normal and Bernoulli families, and transfer to six real datasets (DNA methylation, humidity) with explicit Type-I error checks. The universal single-policy training (500k episodes) is a nice contribution toward practical usability.
The impact statement honestly discusses the interpretability limitation of learned policies, and limitations such as the focus on continuous distributions are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees are only partial and quite conservative. The 'phase diagram' of Figure 1 is explicitly informal; the sufficient conditions involve finite-support distributions (|X| = k), constant-bet policies over the remaining horizon, and correction terms c_T = O(log T / T) that make Propositions 3.4/3.6 hard to satisfy in practice. There is no characterization of the optimal policy in general, and the gap between the theory (finite support, constant bets) and the practical method (continuous distributions, state-dependent bets among three actions) is substantial and not bridged formally.

The empirical Kelly estimate lambda_hat is clipped and used directionally for the 'endpoint/all-in' bet, and the DQN is trained on synthetic Beta/Beta-mixture worlds with a specific difficulty-coupling scheme. There is no formal analysis of how estimation error in the empirical Kelly bet, or distribution shift between training and evaluation worlds, affects performance; generalization claims rest entirely on empirical evidence from a limited family of distributions.

Baseline coverage is limited. The main comparisons are against STaR-Bets/STaR-Hoeffding (adapted by the authors themselves from one-sided to two-sided tests, which could disadvantage the baseline), empirical Kelly, and the authors' own hedged schedule heuristic. There are no comparisons against other horizon-aware or mixture-based e-process constructions (e.g., universal-portfolio betting of Orabona & Jun 2024 adapted to finite horizons, or a Doob-martingale-converted fixed-sample test as in Koning & Van Meer 2026), nor against the oracle DP policy itself, which would contextualize how much headroom remains.

Reproducibility is weakened by a missing code link: page 1 contains a 'Code:' label with no accompanying URL or repository reference, despite heavy experimental content. Hyperparameters are given (Table 1, Appendix E), which helps, but without code, re-implementing the DQN features (22 predictable features described only qualitatively in E.3) and the DP phase-diagram computations would be error-prone.

Several empirical claims are presented from a small number of trials or settings: real-data experiments use 5,000 resampling trials per configuration across only six sources from two domains, with the null mean set relative to the empirical mean; some differences between methods in Figure 3/4 appear modest relative to visible Monte Carlo wiggle, and no error bars or uncertainty quantification are provided on the rejection-probability curves.

The paper claims the DQN 'yields state-of-the-art results' in the abstract, but given the restricted baseline set and the fact that gains depend on a DQN trained on particular synthetic families, this central claim is stronger than the evidence strictly supports; the hedged epsilon-schedule heuristic is a simpler, more interpretable method that is often close in performance, which somewhat dilutes the necessity of the learned policy.

Presentation issues: the theoretical section assumes finite-support distributions for the main propositions while the leading examples and all main experiments use continuous distributions; the connection between the three-action DQN set and the theory is motivational rather than derived; and Figure 1 is a schematic that could be mistaken for a formal result.
